title: Rani Sada Kaur
hook: a widow who led the Kanhaiya misl and backed her young son-in-law, Ranjit

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the misls quarreled: once the danger faded, the bands that had met as the Sarbat Khalsa fought over land and pride. Your line was danger gone, rivalry grew. Did you cool one rivalry? Today, a woman who turned a feud into an alliance. Day nine hundred four.

A betrothal between two families who had lately been at war. That's where today begins. In one of the quarrels between the misls, Sikh histories say, Gurbakhsh Singh, son and heir of Jai Singh of the Kanhaiya misl, was killed in battle, fighting against a coalition that included the Sukerchakia misl. His widow was left with a young daughter, a grieving father-in-law, and a band of riders. You met her earlier in this block. Her name was Sada Kaur. Today: Rani Sada Kaur.
screen: `A BETROTHAL AFTER A WAR.` → `HER HUSBAND KILLED BY THE OTHER SIDE.` → `A WIDOW WITH A DAUGHTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the betrothal. The Sukerchakia chief, Maha Singh, had a son named Ranjit. Sikh histories say Sada Kaur's daughter, Mehtab Kaur, was betrothed to that boy. Hear that again, slowly. Her daughter was promised to the son of the chief her husband had died fighting. Some tellings credit the old chief Jai Singh with the match; in the histories, Sada Kaur is the one who made it work. A marriage turned a feud into a family. That's the first thing to see in her: she could put grief to work for peace. The second is what she did with her place. Day eight hundred ninety-one met her at the head of the Kanhaiya band, commanding its riders and managing its lands. What today adds is how she used that place: not to settle the score, but to build something with the family on the other side of it. The third thing is the one in today's line. Ranjit was young, and there were older, stronger chiefs all around him. Sada Kaur put her men and her judgment behind her son-in-law. When he moved, the histories say, her riders often moved with him, and her counsel went too. The histories give her a large part in his rise. The story doesn't stay sweet. Later, the two would fall out, and that comes in its own time. But at the beginning, when the boy had a name and not much else, there was a woman who had lost her husband in a feud with his family, and who chose to stand behind him anyway. She backed him.
screen: `A FEUD TURNED INTO A MARRIAGE.` · `SHE LED THE KANHAIYA MISL.` · `HER RIDERS BEHIND RANJIT.` · `LATER, THEY WOULD FALL OUT.` · then, large: `SHE BACKED HIM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to back someone young. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a young person in your life: a niece, a student, a new hire, a teenager down the street, your own kid. Think about what they're trying to do right now that's a little bigger than they are. What could you put behind them? Not advice they didn't ask for. Something real: your time, your name as a reference, a ride, a word to the right person, a seat at your table. Choose one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sada Kaur, widow of Gurbakhsh Singh and leader of the Kanhaiya misl, who joined her daughter to Ranjit of the Sukerchakia and put her riders behind him. Today's word.
Your line: she backed him. Today, put something real behind one young person: an hour, a recommendation, a ride, a good word. Day nine hundred four.

notes: Gurbakhsh Singh killed in battle (near Batala, against a coalition of Maha Singh Sukerchakia and Jassa Singh Ramgarhia): framed as 'Sikh histories say'; confirm.
Whether Jai Singh Kanhaiya or Sada Kaur arranged the betrothal: the voice says 'some tellings credit Jai Singh'; confirm.
'The real power in the Kanhaiya misl': confirm the scope; Jai Singh was still alive at first.
'Her riders often moved with him': kept general; the capture of Lahore and other campaigns are left for later lessons. Confirm.
Later falling-out (Ranjit Singh eventually confining Sada Kaur) mentioned only as 'the two would fall out'; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with the forward reference.
Source given generically as Sikh histories of the misl period; a Keeper may prefer a specific history (e.g. Sohan Lal Suri's Umdat-ut-Tawarikh).
